desc:
A directed graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Each entry edges[i] = [a, b] is a one-way edge from a to b. The graph may contain cycles and self-loops.

A topological order is a list that contains every node exactly once and in which, for every edge [a, b], node a appears before node b. You are given a candidate list order of exactly n values, each between 0 and n - 1, but values may repeat. Return true if order is a topological order of the graph and false otherwise.

n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]], order = [0,2,1,3] -> true
n = 4, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]], order = [0,1,3,2] -> false
n = 3, edges = [[0,1]],                   order = [0,1,1]   -> false
constraints: 0 ≤ a, b < n; self-loops and repeated edges are allowed
hints: Two things must hold: every node occurs exactly once, and every edge points forward in the list. Check them one at a time.
To test an edge quickly you need to know where each node sits in order. Build a lookup pos[node] instead of searching the list for every edge.

Fill pos while checking that no node appears twice (this also proves every node appears, because the length is n). Then return false as soon as an edge has pos[a] ≥ pos[b]. A self-loop always fails this test.
editorial: First make sure order is a permutation of the nodes. It has n entries in range, so it is a permutation exactly when no value repeats. While scanning, store the position of each node in pos and fail on a repeat.

Then every edge [a, b] must satisfy pos[a] < pos[b]. If all edges pass, each node's predecessors come before it, which is the definition of a topological order. A graph with a cycle can never pass, because following the cycle would need positions that increase forever; a self-loop fails immediately since pos[a] < pos[a] is false. Total work is O(n + m) time and O(n) space.
